Salve

/SAV/ - rhymes with have · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Salve means a soothing ointment or balm.

Regulars at the climbing gym pass around a homemade salve for torn calluses that smells of mint and motor oil.

Worked Example

After a week of surf lessons, the instructor handed each camper a stick of zinc salve for chapped lips and reef-scraped shins. The stuff works no miracles; what it does is seal the raw spots from salt and sun so the last two days of camp don't hurt.

Salve is the exact noun because it names a soothing ointment — a preparation whose whole job is comfort and protection. Lotion would suggest cosmetics, and medicine overstates it; a salve soothes what it covers. The word also lives a second, figurative life: praise after a defeat can be a salve for wounded pride.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

ointment: An ointment is the pharmacy's neutral word for a medicated cream, and like a salve it does its work at the surface it covers. What a salve adds is warmth and a specific promise: the homely jar that soothes and protects what it seals. Ointment is the clinical label; salve is the comfort.

balm: A balm soothes gently, and the word leans poetic — balms comfort skin or spirits, easing what stings at the surface. A salve is its plainer twin, the everyday jar for scrapes and chapped hands. Both stay mild and stay on top; neither is meant to be driven deep.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

irritant: the thing that makes skin — or a mood — angrier

abrasive: what scrapes and chafes instead of soothing

Where it sits · how deep the treated hurt lies — lotion → salve → liniment

lotion vs. salve: A lotion is the lightest touch — moisture for ordinary skin, with no hurt to treat — a step below a salve, which soothes and shields real damage.

liniment vs. salve: Liniment goes deeper than a salve — a salve soothes and shields the surface, while liniment is rubbed in to reach the ache underneath.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — salve

Root — salve: healing ointment (Old English sealf)

Put it together

Put it together: Nothing peels off here — salve is one solid Old English word, sealf, a healing ointment, and it has meant exactly that for over a thousand years. Beware the look-alike family: save, salvage, and salvation come from Latin salvus ('safe') and are no relation. The spelling drifted toward them, but the old Germanic ointment word was here first.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Old English sealf never grew a family: no prefix comes off, and no other everyday word shares the root. Even the verb use — to salve a guilty conscience — is just the same ointment word put to work on feelings. Its resemblance to save and salvation is coincidence, not kinship.

Strength Check

Word Choice

homey / neutral

Salve is the homely word from the farm kitchen and the first-aid kit, and it carries that warmth into figurative use: an apology can be a salve for hurt feelings. Ointment is the clinical shelf label; balm leans poetic. Note the kinship in meaning — not in origin — with this unit's palliate: both soothe without curing.
